name: Lena Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Lena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I plan campaigns for a natural skincare brand, the face oils and refill pouches you see in chemists. My day is mostly spreadsheets and calls: launch calendars, budgets for influencer posts, briefs for the photographers, and then checking every claim so we don't say "chemical-free" again and get told off. Around four I usually write the email newsletter, which is the bit I secretly like best.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Since a private equity firm bought us last year, everything has to prove its return within a quarter. My boss has to justify every hire, so when Daniel left we just split his work three ways. I use an AI tool now and then, mostly to tidy subject lines or sum up a survey, but only because the rest of the team already did and it seemed to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, because that's roughly what's happening at work right now. We've got a tool that writes ten subject lines, I pick one, and the world carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: AI is a handy helper, but the real story in marketing is owners squeezing teams. I'd probably post about the private equity thing before I'd post about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI wouldn't be my problem in that world; the private equity owners would, because they want the brand ready to sell again in three years. That usually means fewer people. I've got about eight months of savings and some index funds, so I'd be fine for a while, but I'd still be watching the team list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, keep using the subject-line tool, and keep paying into my index funds every month like I do now. I'd also keep my CV warm, because there are plenty of brand jobs in the city if this one goes sour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I think. Not about robots or AI, more about the people with the spreadsheets above us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you it was time to leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they cut the newsletter budget or merge us with the haircare team, I'd start applying that week. Those are the two signals my friend at another brand saw right before her team went.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to about work worries?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Ana, mostly, on Sunday calls. She works for the city council and thinks I'm mad to stay in private companies at all.

say: I'd say AI is a **handy helper**, and the real story is owners **squeezing teams**.
I'd post about the **private equity** owners before I'd post about AI.
think: The danger to my job is the **owners**, who want the brand ready to sell in three years.
My **eight months** of savings and index funds mean I'd be fine for a while.
do: Keep using the **subject-line tool** and running campaigns as now.
Keep paying into her **index funds** every month.
Start applying elsewhere if the **newsletter budget** is cut or teams merge.
feel: **Uneasy**, aimed at the owners with the **spreadsheets**, not at AI.
S0.quote: AI wouldn't be my problem in that world; the private equity owners would, because they want the brand ready to sell again in three years.
fieldNote: Her worry already exists: **private equity** owners pushing for cuts before a resale.
She uses AI **pragmatically** and sees it as minor in this picture.
She has two clear **warning signals** for when she'd start job hunting.

steps.text: Keep using the subject-line tool for the skincare newsletter
Keep paying into her index funds every month
Apply to other brands if the newsletter budget is cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one's the private equity owners' dream. Fewer planners, AI writing the briefs, and someone like me checking the output.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs rules: if a company replaces people with software, the company should pay into retraining the people it replaced. At work I'd ask, politely but on the record, what the plan is for the team, not just the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes before it disappears. Planning and writing are most of my day, so I'd go from making campaigns to reviewing what a tool made, and they'd need fewer of us doing that. I'm average, so I'm not the one they'd fight to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the tools, not just the subject lines, maybe a short course in the first three months, because I've seen they actually work now. I'd join the creative workers' union my friend keeps sending me links to. And I'd start looking at council and charity communications jobs, like the one my sister has, where change seems slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. It feels like a race where I'm not sure what the finish line is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said council jobs change more slowly. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly because my sister Ana's office still faxes things, honestly. But also because public bodies have to explain every change in public, and that buys people time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if your hours or pay dropped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend trips, then the gym I barely go to. I wouldn't touch the index funds unless I had to, because they're my escape route.

say: I'd say firms replacing people with **software** should pay into **retraining**.
At work I'd ask on the record about the **plan for the team**, not just the budget.
think: My job **changes first**: from making campaigns to reviewing what a tool made.
As an **average** planner, I'm not the one they'd fight to keep.
do: Take a short **AI course** in the first three months and use the tools properly.
Join the **creative workers' union** her friend keeps recommending.
Apply for **council and charity** communications jobs like her sister's.
feel: **Anxious** but not frozen, like a **race** with no clear finish line.
S1.quote: If a company replaces people with software, the company should pay into retraining the people it replaced.
fieldNote: She'd adopt the tools now because **others proved** they work, typical of her steady pace.
Her escape plan is the **public sector**, shaped by her sister's slower-moving office.
She protects her **index funds** as an exit route, cutting small luxuries first.

steps.text: Take a short course on AI campaign tools in the first three months
Join the creative workers' union her friend recommended
Apply for council and charity communications jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is brutal. My whole job is thinking work on a laptop, so the robots coming later is irrelevant to me. Maybe the photographers get three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to act now: slow it down, tax it, and protect income for the people it hits. I'd be signing petitions and going to marches, and I'd make sure everyone I know is registered to vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job is gone by the end of 2028, and so is most of the market I'd move into. The council comms plan doesn't work either, because that's thinking work too. I'd have savings for maybe a year if I stopped renting alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give notice on my flat and move in with my sister, which halves my costs straight away. I'd stop all the little spending and keep the index funds as the last thing I touch. And I'd start looking at jobs that need hands, even short term, because those get three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scary. Like the floor's gone and everyone's pretending it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your sister works for the council. How would her job look?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the same as mine, just a bit later because they're slow. So we'd be two people in one flat both wondering what's next, which isn't the most cheerful picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of hands-on work would you even consider?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worked in a bakery all through university, so maybe that. It's early mornings and it pays half what I earn now, but a person still has to shape the bread for a few more years.

say: I'd say governments must **slow it, tax it** and protect people's income right now.
I'd sign **petitions**, go to marches and get everyone I know **registered to vote**.
think: My job is likely **gone by 2028**, and the council plan fails too.
Savings last **about a year** if I stop renting alone.
do: Give notice on the flat and move in with her **sister** to halve costs.
Cut all the **small spending** and keep the index funds as a last resort.
Look for **hands-on work**, like the bakery she worked in at university.
feel: **Scared**, as if the floor has gone and everyone is **pretending** it hasn't.
S2.quote: My whole job is thinking work on a laptop, so the robots coming later is irrelevant to me.
fieldNote: Two years leaves her no **escape route**: her public sector plan collapses too.
She reaches for **hands-on work** she knows, accepting half the pay.
Her **politics** sharpen into petitions, marches and voter registration.

steps.text: Give notice on her flat and move in with her sister
Stop weekend trips and the gym membership
Apply for early-morning bakery work like she did at university
Sign petitions and register friends to vote for AI protections

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is the one where I'd have to be organised. Not panic, just a very serious spreadsheet, which is fine, I live in spreadsheets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window to build a safety net before it lands, like income support and retraining money. I'd probably volunteer for a campaign group on it, because five years is just about long enough for politics to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my marketing job probably lasts three or four of the five years, and then it's done. The real question is what I've built by then. I've got the savings to take a pay cut for a while, which a lot of people don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd use the AI tools properly at work, so I stay useful as long as possible, and save harder towards eighteen months of costs. I'd start a part-time course in something human-facing, maybe counselling or teaching. And I'd join the campaign group for a basic income my sister already volunteers with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. More like nervous before an exam than nervous on a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why counselling or teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Counselling and teaching are jobs where people might still want a person in the room, even if a machine could do the talking. I don't know if that's true, but it's the best guess I've got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots arrive around 2034 in this picture. Does that change anything for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much for me, because I'm not planning a hands-on career. It changes the bakery backup plan, though: that one only works for a few years.

S3.quote: Counselling and teaching are jobs where people might still want a person in the room, even if a machine could do the talking.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **spreadsheet plan**, which suits her.

steps.text: Use AI planning tools fully on the skincare campaigns
Save towards eighteen months of living costs
Start a part-time counselling or teaching course
Volunteer with her sister's basic income campaign group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years feels almost generous after the others. I'd be 37, which is still young enough to start something completely new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got no excuse this time: a decade is enough to build a proper plan for workers. I'd talk about it at work as a reason to train people, not cut them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still assume my marketing job goes, just not soon. Ten years means I could do a full counselling qualification part-time and switch around 32 or 33, before things get bad. That actually sounds like a life, not an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep using the tools, because they'd be part of the work anyway. In year one I'd sign up for a part-time counselling diploma and maybe cut to four days by year three to fit placements. I'd keep investing every month, because ten years of index funds is a real cushion by 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit anxious, because ten years can turn into five very quickly if things speed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if it does speed up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in the five-year picture with a head start, which is still better than nothing. That's why I'd start the diploma in year one, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything in your personal life, like where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. There are plenty of jobs around here, and I like being near my sister. I'd just stop dreaming about a fancy flat and keep renting cheaply.

say: I'd say a **decade** leaves no excuse not to build a plan for workers.
At work I'd argue it's a reason to **train people**, not cut them.
think: My marketing job still **goes eventually**, just not soon.
A part-time **counselling** qualification and a switch at 32 sounds like a life.

Cut to **four days** by year three to fit placements.
Keep **investing monthly** and keep renting cheaply.
feel: Mostly okay, but **anxious** that ten years could **speed up** to five.
S4.quote: Ten years means I could do a full counselling qualification part-time and switch around 32 or 33, before things get bad.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her plan feel like **a life**, not an emergency.
She starts early as a hedge against the timeline **speeding up**.
She'd give up the **fancy flat** dream rather than her investments.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time counselling diploma in the first year
Keep investing in index funds every month
Keep using AI tools for skincare campaigns as they spread

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because every plan I have fails in that one, even the council job. What would help is income support while people retrain, and actual places on courses, not a website with videos.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the owners. In my case the private equity firm worries me as much as the AI does. AI is the tool, but the owners decide what to do with it.

headlineQuote: AI is the tool, but the owners decide what to do with it.
portrait: Lena is a **27-year-old campaign planner** at a natural skincare brand, with eight months saved and index funds.
She uses AI **now and then**, adopting tools once colleagues prove they work.
She already worries about **private equity owners** cutting staff, more than about AI itself.
Faster AGI pictures move her from **uneasy** to **alarmed**, while slower ones become a **retraining plan**.
She blames owners, not technology, and turns to **unions, campaigns and voting**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because every **backup** plan fails, including a council job.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** during retraining and real **course places**, not online videos.
